questions.question: Which technique category matches each type of problem covered in the course?
questions.reference_answer: Grouping by similarity: clustering (k-means); relationships between items/actions: association rules (Apriori); outcome vs inputs: regression (linear regression); assigning known labels: classification (Naive Bayes, decision trees); text data: text analysis (regular expressions, bag of words, TF-IDF).
key_points: text analysis: regex, bag of words, TF-IDF

questions.question: What is the difference between partitional and hierarchical clustering?
questions.reference_answer: Partitional clustering divides objects into non-overlapping subsets so each object is in exactly one cluster; hierarchical clustering produces a set of nested clusters organized as a tree (dendrogram).
key_points: partitional: non-overlapping, each object in exactly one cluster

questions.question: What are the input and output of k-means clustering?
questions.reference_answer: Input: numerical data with a distance metric over the variable space (e.g. Euclidean distance). Output: the centers of each discovered cluster and the assignment of each input datum to a cluster.
key_points: a distance metric such as Euclidean distance
output: assignment of each point to a cluster

questions.question: What are agglomerative and divisive hierarchical clustering?
questions.reference_answer: Agglomerative starts with each point as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the closest pair; divisive starts with one all-inclusive cluster and repeatedly splits until each cluster holds one point (or k clusters remain).
key_points: agglomerative: start with single points, merge closest pair
divisive: start with one cluster, split
use a similarity or distance matrix

questions.question: What are the use cases of the Naive Bayesian classifier?
questions.reference_answer: It is the preferred method for many text classification problems (try it first); use cases include spam filtering, other text classification tasks and fraud detection.

questions.question: What do support and confidence mean in association rules?
questions.reference_answer: Support is the percentage of transactions that contain an itemset; confidence of X -> Y is the percentage of transactions containing X that also contain Y.
key_points: support: % of transactions containing the itemset
confidence: % of transactions with X that also contain Y

questions.question: What is the Apriori property?
questions.reference_answer: Any subset of a frequent itemset is also frequent; this lets the algorithm prune the search space while growing itemsets from size 1 to K.
key_points: any subset of a frequent itemset is frequent
used to prune the search space

questions.question: In the k-means example with K=2, what were the initial centroids and what are the final clusters?
questions.reference_answer: Initial centroids m1 = (1.0, 1.0) and m2 = (5.0, 7.0); the algorithm stops with clusters {1, 2} and {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}.
key_points: stops because assignments no longer change

questions.question: For the Play Tennis example x' = (Sunny, Cool, High, Strong), what does Naive Bayes predict and why?
questions.reference_answer: P(Yes|x') is proportional to 0.0053 and P(No|x') to 0.0206; since P(Yes|x') < P(No|x'), the MAP rule labels x' as 'No'.

Why is adding more clusters not always a sign of a better clustering?
questions.reference_answer: Increasing K is an easy way to reduce SSE, but a good clustering with a smaller K can have a lower SSE than a poor clustering with a higher K.
key_points: SSE always drops as K grows
a good clustering with smaller K can beat a poor one with larger K

questions.question: How do I choose a good number of clusters?
questions.reference_answer: Use the elbow heuristic on the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS) plotted against K; also check diagnostics: decrease K if clusters have few points or centroids are too close, increase K if expected splits are missing.
key_points: elbow of the WCSS plot against K
few points per cluster or close centroids: decrease K

questions.question: How does least squares decide where to draw the regression line?
questions.reference_answer: It chooses a and b so that the sum of squared errors (SSE) between the actual and predicted y is minimum; the errors e are the vertical distances to the line and sum to zero.
key_points: minimizes the sum of squared errors (SSE)
error = vertical distance between actual and predicted y

questions.question: Why would someone use multiple regression instead of a simple regression?
questions.reference_answer: Multiple regression considers several explanatory variables at once, so you can see each variable's independent effect while adjusting out potential confounders; with two predictors it fits a plane in 3-D instead of a line.

questions.question: What does an entropy of 0 or 1 mean for a node in a decision tree?
questions.reference_answer: For binary classification H = 0 is a pure node; H is maximum (1) when the classes are equally likely (50/50).
key_points: entropy is maximum when classes are equally probable

questions.reference_answer: Internal nodes are decisions on a variable, branches are the outcomes of a test, and leaf nodes are class labels.

questions.question: What is an ROC curve, and what is the difference between sensitivity and specificity?
questions.reference_answer: An ROC curve shows a classification model's performance at all thresholds by plotting the true positive rate against the false positive rate. Sensitivity is the true positive rate (recall); specificity is the true negative rate (262/300 = 0.87 in the credit example).
